explainers.title: Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Block Count in LLM Post-Training
explainers.abstract: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. We explain both rules using an analytical model that accounts for update rounding, under assumptions supported by profiling experiments. Finally, we develop two prototypes of the learning rate search for a 6.7-billion-parameter model. The first fits the search on a single consumer GPU with 16 GiB of memory. The second speeds up the search on a high-end GPU by evaluating all candidate learning rates in a single pass over the data, so that a five-candidate search takes about half the GPU hours of one full-depth ($k=L$) run.

summary.tldr: Tune the learning rate cheaply by training only the last transformer block, then use a simple scaling rule that depends on number precision to predict the best rate for full finetuning.
keyPoints: TipSweep searches the learning rate while training only the last k0 blocks (typically one), which is far cheaper than a full-model grid search.
The optimal rate scales about as k^-1 with FP32 master weights, but as k^-1/2 when updates go straight into BF16 weights, which an update-rounding model explains.
Prototypes for a 6.7B model fit the search on a 16 GiB GPU, or test all candidates in one data pass, at about half the GPU hours of one full run.

scenes.caption: Post-training (SFT, DPO, RLVR) is very sensitive to the learning rate, and grid-searching it on the full model is costly.
TipSweep trains only the last $k_0$ blocks (typically one) to find the best learning rate cheaply.
Scaling rules predict the optimal rate for any $k$ blocks, and they depend on weight precision.
Why the difference? Updates applied directly to BF16 weights get rounded, and an analytical model of this rounding explains both rules.
For a 6.7B model, the search fits on a 16 GiB consumer GPU, or runs all five candidates in one pass for about half the cost of one full run.

explainers.title: EEG Decoding in Context: A Framework for Tuning-Free EEG Foundation Models
explainers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding is a central route toward brain-computer interfaces for communication, rehabilitation, cognitive assessment, and neurological monitoring. Recent EEG foundation models have substantially advanced reusable signal representations, but their downstream use still typically requires a task-specific decoder, gradient-based adaptation, and validation-driven model selection. We investigate a complementary foundation-model paradigm based on in-context learning: labeled EEG recordings define the decoding task as context, and new recordings are predicted without updating model parameters. We first pair raw EEG features with a pretrained general-purpose in-context predictor. This direct formulation provides a promising starting point, but its performance remains limited and unstable and does not generalize reliably across EEG paradigms. We find that suitable context construction can address these limitations by improving the effective signal-to-noise ratio and exposing temporal and spatial structure. Building on this insight, we introduce a general framework that combines EEG-specific context construction with a frozen in-context predictor and a metric-based context adaptation mechanism, which matches each downstream task to an appropriate context representation without relying on validation data. Across ten datasets spanning seven EEG decoding paradigms, our method achieves the highest mean BAcc among eleven specialized and fine-tuned EEG baselines, without task-specific parameter updates or validation-based model selection. This framework provides a practical path toward tuning-free EEG foundation models in which adaptation is expressed through context rather than parameter updates.

summary.tldr: Instead of retraining a model for each brain-signal task, this method shows it a few labeled EEG examples and lets a frozen model predict new recordings straight away.
keyPoints: Today's EEG foundation models still need a task-specific decoder, gradient fine-tuning and validation-based model selection for each new task.
In-context learning on raw EEG is unstable; building better context raises effective signal-to-noise and exposes temporal and spatial structure.
A frozen predictor with metric-based context adaptation achieves the highest mean BAcc versus eleven baselines across ten datasets and seven paradigms.

scenes.caption: EEG decoders usually need a new head, gradient fine-tuning, and validation-based model selection for every task.
In-context learning instead: labeled recordings act as context, and a frozen predictor labels new ones without updating parameters.
Feeding raw EEG features directly is a promising start, but results are limited, unstable, and don't transfer reliably across paradigms.
The fix is EEG-specific context construction, which raises effective signal-to-noise and exposes temporal and spatial structure.
A metric-based adaptation step picks the best context representation for each task, with no validation data needed.
Across ten datasets and seven paradigms, it beats eleven specialized and fine-tuned baselines in mean BAcc, with no task-specific parameter updates.

explainers.title: Polynomial mixing for 2D Ising with plus boundary conditions
explainers.abstract: We study the Glauber dynamics of the 2D Ising model at low temperatures. In the absence of boundary conditions, the mixing time on an $n\times n$ box is exponential in $n$ due to a bottleneck between metastable plus and minus phases. When the symmetry is broken via all-plus boundary conditions, it has been predicted in the physics literature since work of Lifshitz (1962) that from an all-minus initialization, the minus droplet shrinks via mean-curvature flow on timescales that are quadratic in $n$, and thus, the system equilibrates in polynomial time. On the rigorous side, the strongest result was a quasi-polynomial mixing time upper bound due to Lubetzky, Martinelli, Sly and Toninelli (2013); a proof of polynomial mixing remained one of the major challenges in the field. We prove this polynomial mixing time bound at all low temperatures. The key step is to establish fast mixing of the interface separating the plus and minus phases on a box with Dobrushin boundary conditions. In simpler models of height functions, polynomial bounds tend to rely on exact harmonic properties and connections to a discrete heat equation. However, the Ising interface exhibits microscopic defects that necessitate the development of a more robust method. We address this via a new multiscale approach to bound mixing times of general disordered random-walk bridges that homogenize to a Brownian bridge at mesoscopic scales. Another notable ingredient is a novel application of censoring to reduce the mixing time problem to proving only a weak Poincaré inequality, or warm-start mixing bound, allowing us to assume suitable regularity conditions on the interface and bubbles.

summary.tldr: A magnet model on a grid, started all 'down' but surrounded by 'up' boundary spins, is proven to settle into equilibrium in polynomial time, confirming a 1962 physics prediction.
keyPoints: Without boundary conditions, low-temperature 2D Ising Glauber dynamics mixes in time exponential in n because of a bottleneck between plus and minus phases.
With all-plus boundaries, the authors prove polynomial mixing at all low temperatures, improving the previous quasi-polynomial bound of Lubetzky–Martinelli–Sly–Toninelli.
Key tools: a multiscale method for disordered random-walk bridges that look Brownian at mesoscopic scales, plus censoring to reduce to a warm-start bound.

scenes.caption: Low-temperature 2D Ising on an $n\times n$ box. With free boundary, flipping from all-minus to all-plus must cross a bottleneck, taking time exponential in $n$.
Add all-plus boundary and start from all-minus. Physics (Lifshitz 1962) predicts the minus droplet shrinks by mean-curvature flow in time about $n^2$.
Key step: with Dobrushin boundary (plus above, minus below), show the interface between phases mixes fast. It has microscopic defects, so exact harmonic tricks fail.
New multiscale method: disordered random-walk bridges that homogenize to a Brownian bridge at mesoscopic scales mix polynomially fast.
Censoring reduces the task to a weak Poincaré (warm-start) bound, letting regularity be assumed. Result: polynomial mixing at all low temperatures.

explainers.title: On-Policy Codec Distillation for Efficient All-in-One Video Generation
explainers.abstract: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.

summary.tldr: Video generators slow down when fed many reference inputs; borrowing the trick video codecs use to skip repeated content, this method drops redundant input tokens and still generates video at nearly the same quality.
keyPoints: Every condition (identity, scribble, depth, motion) becomes tokens appended to the input, so conditioning dominates compute, though much of it is redundant.
A codec-based pruning step keeps only genuinely new spatiotemporal tokens; on-policy self-distillation trains a DiT adapter to work with the pruned input.
Across 16 condition modalities it prunes 66% of condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop, making denoising 2x faster and cutting KV cache memory by up to 73%.

scenes.caption: Every condition (identity, scribble, depth, motion) is tokenized and appended to the sequence. Conditioning quickly dominates the compute.
Most of these condition tokens repeat the same spatiotemporal content from frame to frame.
Key insight: video codecs already know how to identify what is genuinely new. Codec-based pruning keeps only those tokens.
On-policy self-distillation trains a DiT adapter on pruned inputs so its outputs match those of the full-token model.
Across 16 condition types, about 66% of condition tokens are pruned with almost no quality drop. Denoising runs 2x faster and KV cache memory shrinks by up to 73%.
labels: gains grow with more inputs, frames, resolution

explainers.title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
explainers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. Applying CO-GRAFT to Search-R1 agents across Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 models (spanning two sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO optimizers, and NQ and HotpotQA datasets), we show that query generation never exceeds 15% of the total gain; instead, gains are governed by pre-RL answer validity, search retention, model scale, and fixed task-level search budgets, shifting credit from reasoning toward answer extraction in larger or well-formatted answer response checkpoints while smaller base models rely on reasoning--decision coupling.

summary.tldr: RL makes LLM search agents much more accurate. CO-GRAFT swaps control of each step between the trained and untrained model to find which skills actually improved.
keyPoints: Trained and pre-RL policies co-generate one trajectory with live retrieval, each controlling a disjoint subset of four roles, with no retraining.
All 16 role assignments form a cooperative game: Shapley values split the RL gain across roles, and Möbius terms reveal coupling between roles.
Query generation never exceeds 15% of the gain. Credit shifts to answer extraction in larger or well-formatted models, and to reasoning–decision coupling in small base models.

scenes.caption: RL can lift search agents by up to 32 exact-match points. But a single accuracy number hides which capabilities actually improved.
An agent's behaviour splits into four roles: reasoning, deciding to search or answer, writing queries, and extracting the final answer.
In a grafted run, the RL policy and the pre-RL policy share one trajectory, and each controls a different set of roles. No weights are changed.
Scoring all 16 assignments defines a cooperative game. Shapley values split the total gain across roles, and Möbius terms isolate coupling between roles.
Query generation never exceeds 15% of the gain. Larger or well-formatted models gain mostly through answer extraction, while small base models rely on reasoning–decision coupling.

explainers.title: Know When to Abstain: Conformal Confidence Estimation for Text-to-SQL
explainers.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems often return queries that execute successfully but answer the wrong question. Detecting these errors at deployment is hard because execution correctness is defined against a gold query, which exists only in labeled data. We formulate confidence estimation for Text-to-SQL as probabilistic query validation under a latent correctness variable that is observable at calibration time through gold-SQL execution and latent at deployment. Our estimator separates generation from validation. A generator LLM writes and executes the query, and a different critic LLM judges the query and its execution result. The critic's validation and execution-grounded alignment scores are fused with the generator's verbalized confidence, token-level uncertainty, and SQL-structural features in a Random Forest, using two sequential LLM calls. Two calibration steps give finite-sample guarantees. A Learn-then-Test threshold ensures, with probability $1-δ$, that the error rate among accepted queries stays below a user-chosen budget. A conformal p-value bounds the false abstention rate. On Spider we use GPT-OSS-120B as generator and Gemma-4-31B as critic. The estimator obtains an AUARC of 0.899. Without abstention, 22.6% of queries are wrong. With a 15% risk budget ($δ=0.1$), a threshold is certified on all 10 resampled splits, and the system accepts 52.4% of queries on average with 9.1% observed error. Five different critic models give similar results. In a controlled comparison on Spider with Olmo-3-32B as generator, the estimator obtains an AUARC of 89.5, compared with 81.2 for the strongest logit-based baseline. Applied to BIRD without retraining, the confidence scores remain informative (AUROC 0.72, against 0.79 on Spider), but the risk guarantee does not transfer, as expected without exchangeability.

summary.tldr: A Text-to-SQL system that scores its own confidence with a second 'critic' AI and declines to answer when unsure, with statistical guarantees on how often accepted answers are wrong.
keyPoints: SQL queries can run fine yet answer the wrong question; correctness is only known on labeled data, so it is treated as a hidden variable at deployment.
A generator LLM writes the SQL, a separate critic LLM judges it, and a Random Forest fuses their signals into one confidence score.
Learn-then-Test thresholds cap accepted-query error (15% budget held on all Spider splits, 9.1% observed); on BIRD scores stay informative but the guarantee doesn't transfer.

scenes.caption: Text-to-SQL queries often execute fine but answer the wrong question. Without abstention, 22.6% of Spider queries are wrong.
Correctness is defined against a gold query: observable on calibration data, hidden at deployment.
A generator LLM writes and runs the SQL; a different critic LLM judges query and result. A Random Forest fuses all signals.
Learn-then-Test picks a threshold so, with probability $1-\delta$, error among accepted queries stays under the budget. A conformal p-value bounds false abstention.
On Spider: AUARC 0.899; at a 15% budget ($\delta=0.1$) a threshold is certified on all 10 splits, accepting 52.4% with 9.1% error. On BIRD, scores stay informative but the guarantee doesn't transfer.

explainers.title: Matching Under Metric Privacy
explainers.abstract: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $Θ\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.

summary.tldr: When matching private points to public ones, how you represent and randomize the data, and who you trust, decides how much accuracy privacy costs.
keyPoints: Projecting onto the public points' affine span gives a smaller representation that preserves every matching cost, so less noise is needed locally.
With a trusted server, Gumbel matching randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment, achieving the tight Θ(n·min{d, log n}/ε) excess cost.
Experiments suggest d ≈ log n as the switch point: randomize coordinates in low dimension, use Gumbel matching in high dimension.

scenes.caption: We want to match $n$ private points to $n$ public points at minimum total distance, without revealing where the private points are.
Locally, each private point is randomized first. Projecting onto the public points' affine span shrinks the dimension but keeps all matching costs.
With a trusted server, Gumbel matching adds noise to edge costs and releases only the assignment, never the points.
Excess cost over the nonprivate optimum grows like $n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon$, and this rate is tight.
Trust model guides design: locally, use low-dimensional points; centrally, distance-based Gumbel matching is optimal even in high dimension. It also enables private two-sample tests.

explainers.title: CTLink: A Text-Prompted Segmentation Model for Linking Radiology Report Findings to 3D Chest CT Scans
explainers.abstract: Radiology reports describe findings in text only, without visually marking them on the scan, so readers cannot directly see which abnormality each reported finding refers to. We introduce CTLink, a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that segments findings described in a chest CT report. CTLink was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented report findings, including ReXGroundingCTv2, a newly annotated dataset of 1134 scans and 1895 findings with every instance of each finding segmented. On the 200 ReXGroundingCT validation scans, CTLink achieved a hit rate of 0.816, an instance F1 score of 0.456, and a mean Dice score of 0.400, compared with 0.533, 0.175, and 0.234 for VoxTell, a publicly available text-prompted segmentation model (P < .001 for all). On the test set of the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge, an ensemble of seven CTLink models achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) and instance F1 score (0.386) of all 48 participating teams. On 50 test scans segmented twice by independent radiologists, CTLink matched or exceeded inter-rater agreement. Diffuse non-focal findings remained the main limitation, partly because their extent is outlined inconsistently even between radiologists. The CTLink model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/rajpurkarlab/CTLink, and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGroundingCT.

summary.tldr: CTLink reads a sentence from a chest CT report and outlines the matching abnormality in the 3D scan, so readers can see what each finding refers to.
keyPoints: Radiology reports describe findings only in text; CTLink is a text-prompted 3D model that segments each described finding in a chest CT.
Trained on 4123 noncontrast CTs with 9547 segmented findings, including the new ReXGroundingCTv2 dataset in which every instance is segmented.
Beat VoxTell on hit rate (0.816 vs 0.533), instance F1 and Dice. A seven-model ensemble topped the 48-team MICCAI challenge. Diffuse findings remain hard.

scenes.caption: A radiology report lists findings in words, but it never marks where they are in the 3D scan.
CTLink takes a report finding as a text prompt and outputs a 3D mask of every matching abnormality.
It was trained on 4123 noncontrast CTs with 9547 segmented findings, including the new ReXGroundingCTv2 set.
On 200 validation scans, CTLink beat the public model VoxTell on all three metrics ($P<.001$).
A seven-model ensemble led all 48 teams in the MICCAI challenge and matched radiologist agreement. Diffuse findings remain hard.

explainers.title: Agentic AI for Intent Management and Control in Autonomous Communication Networks
explainers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation will help future mobile networks translate high-level network intents into concrete network optimization or control actions. However, existing approaches often focus on intent management and orchestration, leaving the adaptation of underlying network optimization and control functions largely unaddressed. This article proposes a triadic agentic AI framework that co-designs intent management and intent fulfillment through three agents: an interpreter, powered by a language model, that translates and refines intents into machine-readable optimization templates; an optimizer that adapts controller policies to intent specifications; and a controller that performs fast decision-making. We discuss the design space of each agent and how the workflow can be embedded across network architectural domains. Finally, we develop a concrete realization combining a language-model interpreter with Bayesian optimization for the optimizer and multi-objective reinforcement learning for the controller, and evaluate it in a radio resource management case study for differentiated connectivity. Results demonstrate how the agentic AI framework can connect high-level intents with runtime network control, showing adaptability of intent specifications and control policies to service requirements and changing network conditions.

summary.tldr: A team of three AI agents turns plain-language goals for a mobile network into fast, adaptive radio control decisions, closing the gap between what operators want and what the network does.
keyPoints: Prior work handles intent management but rarely adapts the underlying network optimization and control functions; this framework co-designs both.
Three agents: a language-model interpreter builds optimization templates, a Bayesian-optimization optimizer tunes policies, and an RL controller acts fast.
In a radio resource management case study for differentiated connectivity, the policies adapt to service requirements and changing network conditions.

scenes.caption: Operators state high-level intents, but networks need concrete control actions. Existing work manages intents and leaves the control functions unadapted.
The framework uses three agents: an interpreter, an optimizer and a controller. Together they handle both intent management and intent fulfillment.
A language model translates and refines the intent into a machine-readable optimization template.
Bayesian optimization tunes the controller policy to the intent specification. Multi-objective reinforcement learning then makes fast runtime decisions.
In a radio resource management case study, intents and control policies adapt to service requirements and changing network conditions.

explainers.title: Self-Supervised Dataset Distillation via Mutual Information Maximization
explainers.abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to compress a large dataset into a small synthetic one that remains effective for training neural networks. Despite its success in supervised learning, DD remains underexplored in self-supervised learning (SSL), where distilled data must preserve the information needed to learn representations that remain consistent across augmentations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), an efficient SSL dataset distillation approach that optimizes synthetic images to preserve augmentation-invariant information. Specifically, MIPA treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes and uses a frozen encoder to assign real samples to them based on feature similarity. A synthetic dataset that preserves such augmentation invariance should yield stable prototype assignments across multiple augmented views of the same real image. MIPA encourages this by maximizing mutual information between cross-view assignments while avoiding trivial solutions in which all real samples are assigned to only a few synthetic prototypes. Evaluations on image classification benchmarks show that synthetic data generated by MIPA yield higher-quality representations than existing distillation approaches while reducing time and storage demands during distillation.

summary.tldr: MIPA shrinks a big image dataset into a few synthetic images that still teach a network good self-supervised features, by keeping what stays the same when images are augmented.
keyPoints: Synthetic images act as learnable prototypes; a frozen encoder assigns each real image to its most similar prototype.
Two augmented views of the same real image should land on the same prototype, so MIPA maximizes mutual information between cross-view assignments.
The objective avoids collapse onto a few prototypes, and the abstract reports better representations than existing distillation methods with less time and storage.

scenes.caption: Dataset distillation compresses a large dataset into a tiny synthetic one. Here we need it to work for self-supervised learning, where there are no labels.
MIPA treats the synthetic images as prototypes. A frozen encoder assigns each real sample to the prototype it is most similar to.
Two augmented views of one real image should land on the same prototype. Stable cross-view assignments mean the synthetic set captures invariant information.
Mutual information also rewards spreading samples across all prototypes, avoiding the trivial case where everything collapses onto a few.
Result: MIPA's synthetic data yields higher-quality representations than existing distillation methods, while cutting distillation time and storage.

explainers.title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
explainers.abstract: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.

summary.tldr: When AI models solve math step by step and rate their own confidence, they stay confident even when wrong, but a planted low-confidence note can push them to fix mistakes.
keyPoints: Across four open models, verbalized step confidence barely separates mistakes from sound steps (AUROC 0.500–0.561) and stays at 95.1–99.9% at the first error.
Injecting a 10% confidence tag at the error step raises downstream correction by +3.7 to +22.5 points, up to 38.5% with active rethinking instructions.
Injecting doubt on correct steps cuts solve rates by up to 22.8 points, so self-correction is limited by detecting errors, not by repairing them.

scenes.caption: A common trick asks models to state confidence at each reasoning step, hoping a drop will trigger backtracking. That assumes two abilities: monitoring and control.
Four open models, 15,200 math attempts, 2,017 errors isolated, then 27,568 counterfactual continuations at those failure points.
Monitoring fails: at the first error, confidence stays at 95.1–99.9%. Confidence barely separates mistakes from sound steps.
Control works: injecting a 10% confidence tag at the error step raises correction by +3.7 to +22.5 points versus a 95% tag.
But doubt on correct steps makes models discard valid reasoning, cutting solve rates by up to 22.8 points.
The bottleneck is detecting errors, not fixing them: models steer on doubt but can't generate it themselves.

explainers.title: Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations
explainers.abstract: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.

summary.tldr: Integral turns an existing vision-language model into an image generator by making it create images in the same visual 'language' it already uses to understand them.
keyPoints: The core difficulty: understanding and generation usually rely on different visual representations, which keeps the model's knowledge from helping generation.
Abstraction Fusion builds shared visual tokens from multiple layers of the frozen vision encoder; Block-wise MoT adds a light generative stream linked at block boundaries.
Sharing the representation improves generative learning over a separate space with similar reconstruction quality, while pretrained understanding is preserved.

scenes.caption: Unified models try to both understand and generate images. Usually they use two different visual representations, one for each task.
Integral's idea: give understanding and generation one shared visual representation space built from the pretrained model.
Abstraction Fusion aggregates hierarchical features from the frozen vision encoder into shared visual tokens.
Block-wise MoT adds a lightweight generative stream that talks to the VLM only at block boundaries, keeping understanding intact.
In controlled comparisons, a shared space learns generation substantially better than a separate one, despite similar reconstruction fidelity.
